prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val2] SLA tiers (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Tier" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 93px
  col 2: header "Monthly uptime commitment" · longest unbreakable word 80px · one-line width 182px
  col 3: header "Service credit" · longest unbreakable word 48px · one-line width 88px
  col 4: header "Support channels" · longest unbreakable word 68px · one-line width 470px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 597px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 596px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 597px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare SLA tiers by their uptime commitments, service credits, and support channels.","reading":"Readers scan down the tier names, compare uptime and credit values across tiers, and read across each row to see the support included.","groups":["Monthly uptime commitment and service credit are compact, comparable numeric terms of the SLA.","Support channels is descriptive text associated with each tier and needs the most room for natural wrapping."],"keep_intact":["Tier names, especially Mission-critical","Uptime percentages and service credit percentages","Individual words and support-channel terms"],"may_wrap":["Monthly uptime commitment and Service credit headers","Support channels descriptions at spaces or between listed channels","Header wrapping can use height shared across the header row; support text can use height shared across each data row."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[114,145,109,228],"idea":"Keep tier names and the service credit header on one line, while giving support descriptions the largest share and allowing the uptime header to wrap."},{"name":"B","widths":[105,125,90,276],"idea":"Prioritize support descriptions with a wide final column, accepting wrapped headers for the two numeric columns."},{"name":"C","widths":[114,203,100,179],"idea":"Keep the uptime header and tier names on one line, with a narrower support column that produces taller rows."}]}
